A.explanation: Radio waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, so their electric field oscillations perpendicular to propagation can be restricted to one plane.

B.explanation: Sound waves in air are longitudinal with oscillations parallel to propagation, so there is no transverse plane to restrict by polarisation.

C.explanation: Ultraviolet waves are transverse electromagnetic waves and can be polarised like visible light.

D.explanation: X-rays are transverse electromagnetic waves, so they can be polarised despite their very short wavelength.

hints: First sort the four named types - radio waves, sound waves, ultraviolet waves and X-rays - into electromagnetic waves and mechanical waves.
Recall that polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, so it requires a transverse wave.
Check which type has particle oscillations parallel to wave travel with no perpendicular plane to filter, and select that type.
walkthrough: Identify the test: polarisation is possible only if the wave has oscillations perpendicular to the direction of propagation, i.e. it is a transverse wave.

Recall the nature of the electromagnetic members: radio waves, ultraviolet waves and X-rays are all transverse electromagnetic waves with oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to travel.
Therefore those three transverse types have many possible planes of oscillation that can be reduced to one by a polariser.
Consider sound waves: in air sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave where air particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A longitudinal wave has only one line of oscillation along the travel direction, so there is no transverse plane to select and it cannot be polarised.
